name: Japandi
summary: A blend of the Scandinavian room and the Japanese room. Low, heavy wood furniture in pale and dark tones stands in a warm off-white room with wide empty floor; paper light, linen, stoneware and slatted screens give texture, and the tatami ratio of 1:2 orders the plan.

philosophy.core_thesis: Calm comes from emptiness and from a few natural things made by hand and placed with care.
design_principles: Keep furniture low: seats at 38–40 cm and tables at 35–40 cm, so that the eye level of the room drops.
Leave 70% of the floor and 85% of the walls empty.
Hold the ratio 1:2 in rugs, panels, bed platforms and screens, after the tatami mat of 91 x 182 cm.
Pair pale oak or ash with one dark element, such as charred or black-stained wood, at a reflectance difference of 40–50 points.
Use only matt finishes: oiled wood, lime or clay plaster, unglazed or matt-glazed ceramics.
Divide zones with slatted screens of 3 cm battens at 3 cm gaps, not with walls.
Show 1 or 3 objects per surface, asymmetric, with one tall element such as a branch.
anti_patterns: Gloss lacquer, chrome or mirror surfaces
Saturated colour on any surface larger than an object
Tall furniture above 90 cm in the middle of the room
Collections of small objects on open shelves
Printed pattern on textiles or walls

composition.plan_logic: A strict orthogonal plan of low pieces with wide gaps. Rugs and platforms follow the 1:2 tatami ratio, and slatted screens divide the zones.
composition.focal_point: One low piece, such as a platform bed or a stoneware vessel on a plinth, or a window with a branch, placed on a third.

rules.rule: Show one focal object on a third of the back wall, with empty wall around it.
Hold the tatami ratio in the plan: rugs, platforms and screens.
Lower all furniture, so that the room reads from a seated or floor eye level.
Leave the floor and the walls empty; the empty space is the main element of the room.
Repeat slats in screens, wall panels and bed heads at one pitch.
rules.value: 6 cm pitch (3 cm slat, 3 cm gap)

rules.rule: Pair pale wood with one dark element in each view.
Balance a low long mass, such as a sofa or a bed, with one tall slim element, such as a lamp or a branch, on the other third.
Use a slatted screen or a paper panel as a translucent plane between zones.
Show objects in groups of 1 or 3 at different heights; never in pairs.
Keep every piece in the middle of the room below 90 cm, so that the full wall and window read from the door.
Keep wide clear routes between the low pieces.
Give warm off-white the walls, greige textiles and pale and dark wood the secondary share, and clay or black the accents.
Use paper shades and low lamps below 120 cm; hide strip lights under shelves and platforms.
Shoot the room level, with a frontal view with the focal object on the left third.

zoning.circulation: Wide straight routes along the 1:2 grid; screens let a route pass without a door.

palette.distribution: Warm off-white plaster on walls and ceiling; greige linen; pale oak floor and furniture; one dark wood piece; a clay or black accent on a vessel or a lamp.

lighting.strategy: Soft, low and diffuse. Paper shades and hidden strips give pools of light near the floor; shadow is part of the room.
lighting.daylight: Diffuse daylight through linen or paper blinds; the light falls soft on the plaster and no hard sun patch lies on the floor.

layers.position: low over the table, 70 cm above it

layers.source: low floor lamp with a paper shade

layers.position: under a floating shelf or a bed platform

materials.finish: Matt everywhere: oiled or soaped wood, limewash or clay plaster, matt-glazed ceramics.
materials.texture_contrast: Planed wood against rough plaster and woven fibre, at about 1:1.

furniture.silhouette: Low, heavy, rectilinear pieces with thick tops and solid bases; soft edges of 5–10 mm radius; no visible hardware.
furniture.arrangement: Pieces stand against the walls or on one 1:2 rug in the centre; 2–4 pieces per room.
key_pieces: low sofa on a wood frame

textiles.pattern: Plain weaves and slub texture only; one quiet stripe or a sashiko stitch at most.
textiles.windows: Linen sheers or paper blinds that diffuse the daylight.

objects.approach: Objects show the hand of the maker: one stoneware vase, one branch, a stack of 3 books.
objects.grouping: 1 or 3 objects per surface, asymmetric, with one tall element.

implementation.brief: A warm off-white room with a pale oak floor. A low linen sofa on an oak frame and a low oak table stand on a 1:2 jute rug; a slatted screen divides the room, a paper lantern hangs low, and one stoneware vase with a branch stands on a third.
implementation.image_prompt: Japandi living room, warm off-white lime plaster walls, pale oak floor, low linen sofa on a solid oak frame, low oak coffee table, rectangular jute rug, charred black wood cabinet, vertical oak slatted screen, paper lantern pendant hung low, one stoneware vase with a single branch, wide empty floor, soft diffuse daylight through linen blinds, calm, matt, minimal, architectural photograph
implementation.negative_prompt: Gloss, chrome, saturated colour, clutter, pattern, tall furniture, cool light, plastic.
implementation.camera: 35 mm lens, camera at 100 cm (low seated eye), frontal view with the focal object on the left third.
implementation.scene_3d: Room 550 x 450 cm, ceiling 250 cm. Overcast sky through linen at transmission 0.5; one 2700 K paper lantern at 150 cm; one 2200 K LED strip under a platform.
furniture_list: low sofa 220 x 90 x 65 cm, seat 38 cm
dark wood cabinet 160 x 40 x 60 cm

emotion.target_response: Stillness: the viewer breathes out and feels the quiet of a room with nothing extra in it.

avoid_when: The users have many objects that must stay in view.
The brief asks for energy, colour or a party room.

modifiers.how: Raise seat height to 42 cm, add white walls, wool textiles and 3–5 lamps; keep the matt natural materials.
Add travertine, bouclé and a mirrored pair of lamps on one axis; keep the tonal palette and the matt finish.

sources.title: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki, In Praise of Shadows (1933; English translation, Leete's Island Books, 1977)
Trend evidence, cite only: the term spread on image platforms and in retail catalogues from about 2016
